title: What are the principles of assessment and rules of evidence?
description: The principles of assessment and rules of evidence test how competency assessment is run and judged. What each means, AI-era checks and an assessor checklist.
shortAnswer: The principles of assessment and rules of evidence are two sets of tests for competency-based assessment. The principles (fairness, flexibility, validity, reliability) govern how assessment is designed and conducted. The rules of evidence (validity, sufficiency, authenticity, currency) govern each individual judgment: is the evidence relevant, enough, the learner's own, and recent? Australia's vocational regulator sets both out explicitly, and they work as a benchmark for workplace assessment anywhere.
keyTakeaways: The four principles of assessment apply to the assessment system; the four rules of evidence apply to each assessor's judgment about one person.
Validity appears in both lists with different meanings: valid assessment design, and evidence adequate to show the described skills and knowledge.
The Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA) sets both out under Standard 1.4 of the 2025 Standards for Registered Training Organisations, which came into effect on 1 July 2025.
ASQA's current guidance applies the rules to AI use: learners declare AI use, and AI-assisted work is supplemented by explanation, questioning or demonstration.
Outside regulated vocational training the rules are not mandatory, but they give any organization a defensible test for competency decisions.

sections.heading: Where do the principles of assessment and rules of evidence come from?

blocks.text: The clearest current statement comes from Australian vocational education and training (VET) regulation. The Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA) [Assessment Practice Guide](https://www.asqa.gov.au/for-providers/standards-for-RTOs/practice-guides/quality-area-1-training-and-assessment/assessment-practice-guide) sets out Standard 1.4 of the Outcome Standards: the assessment system must follow four principles, and assessors must make "individual assessment judgements that are justified based on" four rules of evidence.

ASQA states that the [2025 Standards for RTOs](https://www.asqa.gov.au/for-providers/standards-for-RTOs/about-the-standards) came into effect on 1 July 2025. The practice guide also links the two lists to tool design: under Standard 1.3, assessment tools must be reviewed before use to confirm that assessment can be conducted consistently with the principles and rules. For the wider regulatory context, see [what the 2025 Standards for RTOs require](/regulations/standards-for-rtos-2025-training-and-assessment). Australia is used here as the example; the logic carries to any [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment).

sections.heading: What does each principle of assessment mean?

blocks.text: The principles describe a fair and accurate assessment system: one that accommodates learner needs, recognizes skills however they were gained, requires practical demonstration, and produces the same outcome whichever assessor is involved.

blocks.caption: Principles of assessment (summarized from ASQA Standard 1.4) and a workplace reading of each
head: Principle
What ASQA's wording requires
Workplace equivalent
rows: Fairness
Accommodates the learner's needs, including reasonable adjustments and reassessment where necessary
Adjustments for disability or language, a published appeal route, and a defined reassessment path
Flexibility
Assesses relevant skills and knowledge regardless of how or where they were acquired
Experienced hires can be assessed directly instead of repeating training
Validity
Includes practical application components so skills are demonstrated in a practical setting
Observation or simulation of the real task, not a quiz alone
Reliability
Evidence is interpreted consistently and outcomes are comparable irrespective of assessor
Written decision rules, assessor calibration, and sampling of decisions

blocks.text: Reliability is the principle most often missing in workplace programs. ASQA's examples include developing evidence criteria (decision-making rules) and monitoring the consistency of assessor decisions on an ongoing basis. The distinction between the two properties is covered in [validity vs reliability in assessment](/compare/validity-vs-reliability-in-assessment).

sections.heading: What does each rule of evidence ask of the assessor?

blocks.text: Each rule of evidence is a question the assessor must be able to answer yes to before recording a competency decision. Sufficiency, for example, is met when "the quality, quantity and relevance of the assessment evidence enables the assessor to make an informed judgement" (ASQA, Standard 1.4).

blocks.caption: The four rules of evidence as assessor questions (original analysis based on ASQA Standard 1.4)
head: Rule
Question for the assessor
Typical check
Common failure
rows: Validity
Does this evidence show the skills and knowledge the standard describes?
Map each piece of evidence to the requirement it covers
Evidence of attendance offered as evidence of ability
Sufficiency
Is there enough evidence, of enough quality, across enough situations?
Count observations and contexts against the plan
One observed task used to sign off a role that varies widely
Authenticity
Is this the learner's own original and genuine work?
Identity check, declarations, follow-up questioning
Written work accepted without confirming who produced it
Currency
Does this evidence show what the learner can do now?
Date every item and compare with the procedure version in force
Old certificates accepted after the procedure or equipment changed

sections.heading: How do the rules of evidence apply to AI-assisted work?

blocks.text: ASQA's practice guide treats generative AI as a risk to authenticity, validity and currency, and expects assessment to be designed so the learner's own competence is still demonstrated. Its examples include:

items: **Authenticity:** requiring learners to declare any AI use and having a process to identify inappropriate or undisclosed use.
**Validity:** requiring AI-generated content to be supplemented with the learner's explanations or demonstrations.
**Sufficiency:** adding evidence such as oral questioning or practical demonstration to supplement AI-assisted work.
**Currency:** confirming that evidence reflects current ability, "not outdated or generic AI-generated content".
**Validity as a principle:** designing tasks so that AI cannot replace the skill being assessed, for example hands-on practical tasks.

blocks.text: Video is treated the same way. ASQA's FAQ advises that for work placements, recordings are best used as supplementary evidence rather than a substitute for direct observation, backed by identity checks and assessor questioning.

sections.heading: Do the rules of evidence apply outside vocational education?

blocks.text: Legally, Standard 1.4 binds Australian registered training organizations, not employers. In practice, the same four questions are what an auditor or regulator in any market asks of a competency record. The ISO 9001 Auditing Practices Group, for example, warns in its [guidance on auditing competence](https://committee.iso.org/files/live/sites/tc176/files/PDF%20APG%20New%20Disclaimer%2012-2023/ISO-TC%20176-TF_APG-Competence.pdf) that participation in a course "does not necessarily provide evidence that the trainee is competent", which is a validity problem in the terms above.

Applying the rules internally means writing them into the assessment plan: which evidence covers which requirement, how much is enough, how authorship is confirmed, and how old evidence may be. The broader question of which evidence types count is covered in [what counts as evidence of competence](/glossary/evidence-of-competence), and planning assessments is covered in [how to design competency assessments](/guides/how-to-design-competency-assessments).

sections.heading: How can an assessor check evidence against the four rules?

blocks.text: Illustrative checklist, written for workplace assessors and drawn from the ASQA wording and examples:

items: List the requirements of the standard and map each piece of evidence to at least one (validity).
Confirm every requirement has evidence, including any required number of repetitions or contexts (sufficiency).
Confirm the learner's identity and record any declared AI or other assistance (authenticity).
Ask follow-up questions on any written or recorded evidence the assessor did not see produced (authenticity).
Date each item and check it against the current version of the procedure or standard (currency).
Apply the written decision rule and record the decision, the evidence relied on and the assessor's name (reliability).
Record reasonable adjustments made and tell the learner how to appeal or be reassessed (fairness).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry attaches evidence requirements to each assessment point in the framework, so the type, amount and maximum age of evidence are defined before any assessment is built. Each decision record then shows which requirement each piece of evidence satisfies, which makes validity, sufficiency and currency reviewable.

faqs.q: Why does validity appear as both a principle and a rule of evidence?
faqs.a: They operate at different levels. The validity principle is about the assessment design: it must include practical application so skills are demonstrated in a practical setting. The validity rule is about the evidence in a particular case: it must be adequate for the assessor to be reasonably assured that this learner has the skills and knowledge described.

faqs.q: How old can evidence be before it fails the currency rule?
faqs.a: ASQA does not set a fixed age. Its guidance asks assessors to consider the time that has passed since the evidence was generated and whether it reflects current ability. Organizations usually set their own limit per competency, shorter for fast-changing or high-risk tasks, and treat any change to the procedure as resetting currency.

faqs.q: How often must assessment be validated against these rules?
faqs.a: Under the 2025 Standards, ASQA states that registered training organizations must validate assessment practices and judgments at least once every five years for every training product on scope, and more often where risks, changes to the training product or relevant feedback arise. Workplace programs can adopt a similar cycle.

faqs.q: Is a supervisor's report sufficient evidence on its own?
faqs.a: Usually not. A third party report is indirect evidence, so it rarely satisfies sufficiency alone. ASQA's guidance on work placements recommends supporting supplementary evidence with assessor questioning, workplace documentation or supervisor observations. Combining a report with direct observation or questioning gives a stronger basis for the judgment.
